extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim limitations (additional elements) integrate a recited judicial exception into a practical application such that the claim is not directed to the judicial exception under the Alice/Mayo framework (MPEP § 2106.04(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed subject matter's characteristics are innate to a naturally occurring material and are not markedly different from its natural counterpart, the claim is a product of nature exception and is ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: primers that maintain the exact same nucleotide sequence as natural DNA (In re BRCA1/2; Ambry Genetics) were held products of nature because their ability to serve as starting materials was innate to DNA; ductile vanadium (In re Marden) was ineligible because ductility is an inherent characteristic; cloned animals that are exact genetic replicas (Roslin/Dolly) lacked markedly different characteristics. Alleged phenotypic differences (e.g., height, weight) do not make the clone markedly different if those differences are not claimed. Structural differences not claimed are generally irrelevant (see Roche v. Cepheid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim as a whole integrates a recited judicial exception into a practical application when the claim applies, relies on, or uses the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the exception so the claim is more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If integration is present, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If not, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires further Step 2B analysis. Examiners should use the listed considerations to evaluate integration (see subsequent rubric entries) and follow the procedure described (identify additional elements; evaluate individually and in combination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: improvement in functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element (or combination) that demonstrates an improvement in the functioning of a computer, or an improvement to another technology or technical field, indicates the claim integrates the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the specification to determine if disclosure provides sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill would recognize the claimed invention as providing the improvement; the specification need not explicitly state the improvement but must make it apparent to one skilled in the art. The claim must reflect the components or steps that provide the improvement (it need not literally recite 'thereby increasing the bandwidth'). At Step 2A, do not consider whether the improvement is over well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Examples of eligible improvements: Enfish (self-referential table), McRO (automatic lip synchronization), Visual Memory (enhanced memory), Finjan (virus scanning improvement), SRI v. Cisco (network monitoring). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for further detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: applying/using the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that applies or uses the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition may integrate the exception into a practical application and render the claim not directed to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This consideration is particularly relevant to diagnostic/therapeutic claims. Example: Vanda — claims reciting genotyping and administering a drug in a genotype-dependent dose were held eligible because the steps used the natural-law relationship to safely treat patients rather than merely gather data. Treatment/prophylaxis examples include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, etc. Distinguish from Mayo where administering a drug was ancillary/diagnostic rather than therapeutic in effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: implementing the exception with or using it in conjunction with a particular machine or manufacture integral to the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim implements the judicial exception with a particular machine or manufacture that is integral to the claim, that may show the exception is integrated into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the particular machine/manufacture is integral (not merely incidental). Specific embodiments and how the machine is used should be considered in light of the specification and claim language. Specificity of how the machine is invoked can be relevant (see specificity rubric). See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: effecting a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing is a meaningful limitation that can integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed steps produce a physical transformation or meaningful change in the article. See MPEP § 2106.05(c) for application and examples. Physical steps alone are not automatically sufficient; evaluate how the transformation is tied to the claimed exception and whether it meaningfully limits the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: applying or using the judicial exception in some other meaningful way beyond mere linkage to a technical environment
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim applies or uses the judicial exception in a meaningful way beyond generally linking it to a particular technological environment or field of use, that may indicate integration into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all category for meaningful uses that do more than attach the exception to a technical field. The claim must be more than a drafting effort to monopolize the exception. See MPEP § 2106.05(e) for examples and further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: merely reciting 'apply it' or implementing on a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely reciting the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer, or merely using a computer as a tool to perform an abstract idea does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recitations are insufficient to impose a meaningful limit on the exception (see MPEP § 2106.05(f)). Examiners should look for more substantive interactions between the exception and claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: adding insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding insignificant or conventional extra-solution activity to the judicial exception does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insignificant post-solution activity that merely appends routine steps to an abstract idea or law of nature will not render the claim eligible (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). However, note that at Step 2A examiners should not exclude consideration merely because an element is conventional (see separate rubric on conventionality exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: generally linking the exception to a technological environment or field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally linking the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, without more, does not integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that only identify a field or environment but do not meaningfully apply the exception within that environment are insufficient (see MPEP § 2106.05(h)). The analysis should focus on whether the linkage is meaningful and imposes a limit beyond mere field-of-use language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A limitation: do not consider well-understood, routine, conventional activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong Two specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should give weight to all additional elements, whether or not they are conventional, when evaluating integration into a practical application. Additional elements that are well-understood, routine, conventional activity may nonetheless integrate a recited judicial exception into a practical application under Step 2A (distinct from Step 2B conventionality inquiry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/physicality is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physicality or tangibility of an additional element or elements is not a relevant consideration in Step 2A Prong Two; physical implementation does not guarantee eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court and Federal Circuit have made clear that physical implementation alone (e.g., running an abstract idea on a computer, performing DNA amplification steps) is not sufficient to render a claim eligible. Conversely, non-physical or intangible improvements may still integrate the exception if they meaningfully improve technology or the claimed process (see Alice, Genetic Technologies, Enfish, McRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of claim limitations matters
rubrics_metrics.description: The specificity of claim limitations is relevant to the evaluation of whether additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, including whether the claim uses a particular machine, effects a transformation, or merely instructs to apply an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere recitation of a broad result is less persuasive than limitations that explain how to achieve the result. Lack of disclosure about how to implement claimed steps (e.g., Parker v. Flook — failure to explain selection of variables or monitoring means) can indicate that additional elements are insignificant post-solution activity. See MPEP §§ 2106.05(b), (c), (f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation procedure: identify additional elements and evaluate individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine if additional elements integrate a judicial exception into a practical application, (1) identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and (2) evaluate those elements individually and in combination using the listed considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all considerations will apply to every claim; more than one consideration may be relevant to an element. The analysis is not a weighing test — number or type of considerations is less important than whether the additional elements meaningfully limit the exception. Evaluate the significance of the additional elements relative to the invention and whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP §§ 2106.04(d) and 2106.05(a)-(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-specific examination (each claim evaluated separately)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should examine each claim for eligibility separately based on the particular elements recited therein; claims should not be judged to automatically stand or fall with similar claims in an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One claim may be ineligible as directed to a judicial exception while a dependent claim reciting additional meaningful elements may be eligible. Consider each claim's full limitation set and how those limitations interact when evaluating integration into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement-evaluation detail: sufficiency of specification and claim reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether a claim shows an improvement in technology, the specification must provide sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill would recognize the improvement (not merely conclusory), and the claim itself must reflect the disclosed improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not use the word 'improvement' but must disclose enough detail for the improvement to be apparent. A conclusory assertion of improvement without detail should not lead the examiner to find that the claim improves technology. The claim should include the components or steps providing the improvement, though it need not explicitly state the improvement in result-oriented language. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of judicial decisions and examples to inform analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should consider judicial precedent and examples (e.g., Solutran, Finjan, Vanda, Enfish, McRO) to inform whether additional elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate how courts have applied considerations: e.g., Solutran (claims to crediting merchant before scanning were long-standing practice and not an improvement), Finjan (security profile provided technical improvement and was eligible), Vanda (genotype-based dosing used law of nature to treat patients and was eligible). Use these as analogies when relevant but focus on claim-specific facts and the MPEP considerations.
